newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland should levy special flood tax - govt analyst.
newsitem.headline: Poland should levy special flood tax - govt analyst.

text.p: Poland should choose a temporary "flood tax" as the main source of financing the rebuilding of areas hit by a week-long deluge because it will mobilise substantial funds without widening the budget deficit and public debt, a senior government analyst said on Monday.

Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at the Strategic Studies Centre (CSS) told Reuters in an interview other alternatives now considered by the government would either boost public debt or increase money supply.
"The proposal of a universal tax levied on all households will not hurt the budget, while increasing the public debt, either domestic or foreign, will have negative effects," Chroscicki said.

Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Monday the goverment would ask parliament this week to authorise it to borrow $300 million more abroad than originally planned and to sell one billion zlotys worth of T-bills to the central bank to ease possible problems with deficit financing.
Earlier the government signalled it was contemplating national borrowing because of the floods which inundated up to 4,000 sq km and several cities in southern provinces and claimed 36 lives.
Chroscicki said such measures would either boost public debt and future debt financing costs, or money supply, and in either case would threaten Poland's ambitious inflation targets.

He said the costs of reconstruction, which the government has yet to assess, would probably be most visible in public finances and he expected the flood to leave overall farming and industrial output and overall growth largely unaffected.

"About 240,000 hectares of fields went underwater out of a total of more than 18 million so we are talking about 1.3 percent of the total area so this will not threaten overall food supplies or affect prices," he said.

He said that aside from a few notable exceptions the floods spared most of Poland's large industrial companies which account for most of industrial output. He also said an expected construction boom in the southern provinces should offset any losses of output in the manufacturing sector.

Chroscicki said however Poland's trade deficit might widen more than originally anticipated as the reconstruction efforts would create additional domestic demand attracting both more imports and attract goods which otherwise would be exported.
The Polish economy was expected to grow by 5.5 percent both this year and next while its trade deficit fuelled by booming domestic demand is expected to reach $12 billion at the end of this year.
